title: Inclusive Design: Building for Everyone by Designing for the Edges
description: A short lesson to help you apply Inclusive Design: Building for Everyone by Designing for the Edges.

climax.text: Voice interfaces, dark mode, autocomplete, and touch screens all originated from accessibility needs.

punchline.text: Design for exclusion. Innovation for everyone follows.

quiz.question: What are Microsoft's three types of exclusion in inclusive design?

details.summary: Inclusive design starts by designing for people with the most extreme needs, then discovers that those solutions work better for everyone. Curb cuts designed for wheelchairs help parents with strollers, delivery workers, and travelers with luggage. Edge cases reveal universal opportunities.
details.whyItMatters: Inclusive design produces universally better products while serving communities that are typically excluded. It transforms constraints from limitations into innovation opportunities.
takeaways: Designing for extreme users creates solutions that benefit everyone
Curb cuts, closed captions, and voice control all began as accessibility features
Inclusive design is good business because it expands the addressable market

faq.question: What is the curb cut effect?
faq.answer: The curb cut effect describes how features designed for disabled users end up benefiting everyone. Wheelchair ramps help anyone with wheels. Closed captions help people in noisy bars. Designs for the margins improve the mainstream.

faq.question: Is inclusive design expensive?
faq.answer: It is cheaper to include accessibility from the start than to retrofit later. Inclusive design also expands market reach to the one billion people worldwide with disabilities. The business case often makes it cost-negative rather than cost-positive.
